LLMs are trained over years, so any single tactic has a minor effect; in the example the model moved from 9+ months to 6 months over roughly two years — an improvement, not the target figure.", "Test the result without a web search enabled to see whether the model has absorbed the correction at all.", "Treat related off-site profiles as part of the same repair job: G2, Reddit, Trustpilot, local directories and local board-of-trade listings — update them so the stale claim is not being reinforced elsewhere."], "caveats": ["The source says it has seen no true, verifiable case study of a company reliably entering training data through content volume; the demonstrated result here was partial and slow.", "Model training cut-offs and behavior change frequently — verify current model behavior rather than assuming a fixed timeline."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "training-data", "brand-reputation", "content-distribution", "g2", "trustpilot"]}, {"title": "Diagnose whether an AI answer came from the web or from training data", "summary": "Run the same query in free/incognito and logged-in/paid sessions and inspect citations to see whether the assistant searched the web at all.", "use_when": "Deciding whether to invest in training-data/brand work or web-page optimization for a given set of shopping or brand prompts.", "steps": ["Run an experiment anyone can do: search a prompt in the free version of ChatGPT, then run the same prompt in a separate incognito tab and in a paid/logged-in account, and compare the answers side by side.", "Repeat a few times and reword the sentence structure between runs to see how stable the answer is — the source notes answers shift with phrasing.", "Check for citations. The source repeatedly found that free-version ChatGPT often does not trigger a live web search, so prompt trackers return screenshots with no citations — useless data.", "Use the pattern you observe to allocate effort: if the model answers without searching and repeats a stale fact, prioritize training-data/brand-consistency work; if it searches, prioritize making the retrieved pages strong.", "A cautionary example from the source: a model that had not searched the web still said Trudeau was Prime Minister of Canada a year after he left office — evidence of how stubborn un-searched training data is."], "caveats": ["Model behavior, paywalls and search triggers change often — re-run the experiment before making decisions.", "The source's observations were made at a specific point in time and are not a permanent characterization of any AI product."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "measurement", "chatgpt", "prompt-tracking", "citations", "experiment-design"]}, {"title": "Prompt trackers: understand their limits before trusting AI visibility data", "summary": "Automated AI prompt trackers can report inflated or meaningless visibility when answers vary run-to-run or the model never searched the web.", "use_when": "Reviewing an AI visibility report from a tool, agency or in-house dashboard to decide whether the store is actually being recommended.", "steps": ["Recognize how these tools work: they capture screenshots of a tracked prompt's answer inside ChatGPT or another assistant and upload them for comparison.", "Know the failure mode: if the assistant does not trigger a web search, there are no citations in the answer, so the screen contains no useful evidence of visibility.", "Treat citation counts with suspicion. The source argues citations are easy to inflate — one URL can be cited for an infinite number of branded term variations (e.g. 'how to get rid of mold brand name'), so 'we increased citations' does not mean 'we increased visibility'.", "Recognize that answers vary dynamically; a single tracked prompt is not a stable measurement.", "When reviewing reports, ask which prompts are commercially meaningful to the store, whether web search actually fired, and whether the reported change maps to revenue rather than mention counts."], "caveats": ["The source's view is that the whole citation-measurement system is of questionable value and partly vendor-driven; treat dashboard metrics as directional at best.", "Trackers and assistants change interfaces and behavior — verify the current mechanics before relying on any single metric."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "prompt-tracking", "measurement", "citations", "ai-visibility", "reporting"]}, {"title": "Verify claimed Reddit influence before paying for Reddit GEO", "summary": "Test which Reddit threads actually influence the prompts you care about — often none you can join, and some are locked.", "use_when": "Being pitched a Reddit-mentions service for your store, or considering building a Reddit presence for AI visibility.", "steps": ["Take the keywords and conversational prompts that matter commercially to the store and run them through an SEO or GEO tool to see the specific Reddit URLs being cited by AI for those prompts.", "Identify the subreddits involved and check their rules: the source notes some high-engagement subreddits ban your account the moment a brand name is mentioned, even in a genuinely helpful answer.", "Accept dead ends quickly. In the source's example, the only cited Reddit thread for a bathroom-vanity query was eight years old and locked — creating fifty new pages could not break into that answer.", "If a vendor claims 'increased Reddit mentions', ask what influence that had on the answers you care about. The source warns that many vendor Reddit posts are autogenerated, add no value, and receive no engagement.", "Prefer publishers that already hold AI citations over chasing new Reddit threads that no model currently references."], "caveats": ["Reddit is genuinely cited by AI assistants, per the source, but that does not mean any given Reddit tactic works for any given query.", "Subreddit rules and AI citation sources change over time — re-verify which threads are actually referenced."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "reddit", "off-site-seo", "citation-sources", "vendor-evaluation", "community"]}, {"title": "Get listed in the third-party listicles AI already cites", "summary": "Find the affiliate review pages and listicles that influence your priority prompts and get your brand placed in those, not in new ones you create.", "use_when": "Building off-site AI visibility for a store in a category where comparison listicles (supplements, mattresses, credit cards, fragrances, software) drive AI answers.", "steps": ["Use your GEO or SEO tool's 'sources' section to see which third-party URLs influence the AI answers for your priority prompts; these tools typically flag sources where you are not mentioned.", "Skip competitor-owned listicles — the source states it will not email a competitor asking to be added, and ignores such requests when received.", "Target durable, high-authority publishers in your vertical (the source cites examples like Healthline, WebMD, Sleepopolis for mattresses, large credit-card affiliates) and try to join their affiliate programs, even at a higher cost than you would like.", "For smaller or niche blogs that turn out to be influencing many of your prompts, simply email and ask what it would cost to be included — the source describes this as a straightforward paid placement, sometimes very cheap, that can win citations across many prompts.", "Run the same analysis on competitors: use link/backlink intersection analysis to see which listicles and guest posts they appear in, then pursue the equivalent for your brand — bigger publications for bigger companies, local or cheaper sites for local players.", "Remember the affiliate is often a different team from SEO, so if you run or influence the affiliate program, coordinate with them directly."], "caveats": ["The source notes an unethical variant — companies sponsoring or buying listicles on third-party news sites (it cites a hair-transplant listicle in a Canadian newspaper and law-firm pages) — and explicitly does not recommend or condone it; disclosure requirements vary by industry and jurisdiction.", "Affiliate programs sometimes test placement and click-through rate before giving premium positions."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "off-site-seo", "affiliate-marketing", "listicles", "citations", "backlink-analysis"]}, {"title": "Rank category and product pages for bottom-of-funnel queries without building listicles", "summary": "Your own category and product pages can capture high-intent queries and get cited by AI, without any third-party placement.", "use_when": "Deciding what to build next on-site for AI visibility — a new blog post or an optimized commercial page.", "steps": ["Put up product and landing pages that target high-intent terms directly, and cover the use cases and services you offer — the source describes these as being cited heavily in AI answers, and calls the tactic fully ethical.", "Use e-commerce category page conventions the source observed: a fragrance site's category page can carry the title and H1 'best fragrances for men' while still presenting the normal product grid — no article required to rank for a bottom-of-funnel query.", "Apply the same pattern to service pages: a service page can be optimized for a scenario-driven query rather than written as a blog post.", "Use borrowed credibility where it is legitimate: the source describes a law firm that earned a ranking from a legal publication's affiliate program, then published a page citing that recognition, and subsequently appeared for 'best personal injury lawyers in Canada'.", "Prioritize commercial pages over explainer content; the source observes many competitive commercial keywords (e.g. 'personal injury law NYC') have surprisingly few sites targeting them properly, despite high cost per click."], "caveats": ["The borrowed-credibility example is a third-party recognition placement; check advertising and endorsement disclosure rules in your industry and market.", "SCALE the approach with judgment — the value comes from targeting genuinely searched queries, not from generating pages for their own sake."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "product-page", "category-pages", "bottom-of-funnel", "landing-page", "seo"]}, {"title": "Treat GEO as a company-wide function, not a single marketing hire", "summary": "Because AI answers draw on product quality, reviews, PR, social and support channels, one person cannot fix AI visibility alone.", "use_when": "Scoping who owns AI search performance at your store and setting cross-team responsibilities.", "steps": ["Map the owners: product quality (bad products generate bad Reddit sentiment regardless of optimization), brand reputation and executive conduct, communications/PR messaging, review profiles (Trustpilot, G2, Glassdoor), affiliate relationships, and web content.", "Fix the underlying substance first: if the product or service is genuinely poor, the source is explicit that no amount of Reddit or listicle optimization will overcome what customers say about it publicly.", "Align messaging across channels. If the company has been known for one thing for 15 years and wants to be known for something else, a press release alone will not change what AI says — sustained promotion across many channels is required.", "Use review profiles as a lever: in the source's example, a law firm improved its Glassdoor rating above four stars by encouraging employee reviews, after which ChatGPT stopped using Glassdoor as its review source. The same logic applies to Trustpilot for consumer brands.", "Ensure the affiliate, PR and content owners are coordinate-able, since the cited sources often sit outside SEO's control."], "caveats": ["The Glassdoor example is an anecdote about one firm and one model's source selection at a point in time, not a repeatable guarantee.", "Encouraging reviews must comply with platform policies and applicable law; the source mentions incentives without addressing compliance."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "brand-reputation", "cross-functional", "reviews", "trustpilot", "glassdoor", "pr"]}, {"title": "Update the sources that feed un-searched model answers about your brand", "summary": "When a model answers about your brand without searching, it is drawing on sources like G2, Reddit or directories — correct those sources directly.", "use_when": "An AI assistant gives an outdated answer about your store's policies, pricing, product capabilities or review sentiment without performing a web search.", "steps": ["Identify the likely source by the wording: in the source's example, the model's '9+ months implementation' phrasing traced directly to years-old G2 reviews using similar language.", "Prioritize 'brand + reviews' and 'brand vs brand' prompts. The source notes that for reviews the model typically goes to a review site, so optimize those profiles: encourage positive reviews, and reply to negative ones where the platform allows.", "For local businesses, update directory and local board-of-trade listings — these are the kinds of sources the source names as feeding training data.", "Redistribute the corrected claim beyond the profile itself: onto your website, into third-party articles, and into social video from the founder, as in the case study that moved the answer from 9+ months to 6 months.", "Re-test with web search disabled, since that is the only way to see what the model itself believes."], "caveats": ["The source is explicit that it has not seen a truly verifiable case study of a company deliberately entering training data — the demonstrated effect was partial and took roughly two years.", "Which sources feed which model is not published and changes over time; treat the G2/Reddit/directory list as the source's working hypothesis."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "training-data", "reviews", "brand-reputation", "g2", "local-seo"]}, {"title": "Test whether an AI answer is naming your brand or only linking your page", "summary": "A citation is not the same as a mention — being linked while a competitor is named is not a win for the store.", "use_when": "Reviewing an AI visibility report or checking a Google AI overview for your category to judge whether the visibility claimed is worth anything.", "steps": ["Run your priority queries and read the AI answer carefully. The source describes a case where an AI FP&A software company was cited in Google's AI overview but not named — the answer listed other companies as best and merely linked to their page.", "Interpret the two outcomes differently: a mention puts your brand in front of the buyer; a bare link may just position you as a source that recommends rivals.", "When a vendor reports growth in 'AI visibility', ask whether it is mentions or citations, and which prompts, before treating it as progress.", "Watch for site-scoped searches in the fan-out. The source observed ChatGPT temporarily issuing searches like 'site:G2.com "company name"' — evidence that assistants are actively working to improve answer quality and may bypass self-authored listicles.", "Use the finding to decide whether to invest in being mentioned inside trusted publishers rather than in publishing your own listicle that names you first."], "caveats": ["The site: operator behavior was observed during a limited window and may have been a test; re-verify current behavior.", "Google AI overviews and assistant answers change format often."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "measurement", "citations", "ai-overviews", "listicles", "buyer-visibility"]}, {"title": "Judge AI-visibility tactics by whether they optimize for the user's best answer", "summary": "The durable test for any GEO tactic is whether it improves the experience of searchers, not whether it produces a spike in tracked mentions.", "use_when": "Deciding whether to adopt a specific AI-visibility tactic — self-authored listicles, scaled comparison pages, paid placements — for your store.", "steps": ["Apply the source's test question to each tactic: does this give a user who lands on the page through Google or an AI search engine the best possible experience?", "Use it to reject the spammy version of a legitimate tactic. Comparison pages have existed in legitimate form for years (mattress brand A vs brand B); the GEO version is scaling them to the point of comparing brands nobody searches for.", "Apply the same test to self-authored listicles that place your own company first — they may still rank and be cited, but the source frames them as a tactic that assistants are actively working around.", "Prefer the version of the tactic that serves real intent: your own product, category and comparison pages that answer genuine buyer questions (see the bottom-of-funnel page card).", "Use it as the tiebreaker when a vendor presents a case study: ask whether the pages in question help buyers or simply exist to capture a fan-out variation."], "caveats": ["This is the source's stated ethical/strategic frame, and it explicitly names some effective-but-unethical tactics it does not recommend.", "'Best possible experience' is a judgment call — apply it consistently rather than as a rhetorical test."], "tags": ["answer-and-generative-engines", "content-strategy", "comparison-pages", "listicles", "tactic-evaluation", "user-intent"]}]}

s and AI tools, analyzing prompt rank tracking limitations, tracking search query fan-outs, and monitoring third-party citation sources. modules: [MEA] topics: [seo analytics, rank tracking] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. seo analytics / Evaluating and tracking AI visibility performance by analyzing LLM citations, third-party affiliate sources, and search engine query fan-outs across tools like ChatGPT and Perplexity. Analyzing prompt tracking data and recognizing the limitations of tracking automated AI answers when models do not consistently execute web searches or when result outputs vary dynamically.

Look for. The definition of query fan-out: when an AI tool takes a single search query and expands it into multiple background variations. The measurement risk of automated AI prompt trackers: encountering useless data or missing citations when LLMs process responses without triggering live web searches.

Skip. Strategic debates regarding the safety of automated content scaling (avoiding "Mount AI" rank-and-tank penalties), discussions on influencing training data via press releases, and general critique of agency grifters.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 5 to 10.

We are talking about generative engine optimization. If it is safe with the primary ways that it is being done and then is there actually a right way to do it that is not going to get a website absolutely destroyed where they're losing all of their organic traffic and if they're losing their organic traffic then they're not going to they're not going to be found by large language models and that's what we're talking about. Harpre Singh is joining the show once again. Harpre thank you for being here. Thanks for having me back. >> Uh, all right. So, let me ask you, is generative engine optimization the top ways that it is being done? Is it safe? >> Yeah. Um, so I think that there's a few different ways you can do um, GEO. One of the ways that is being recommended, the most popular method is just publish more content. Make keywords for the query fan out. So, you know, in case the listeners aren't aware what query fan out is, when you make a search inside of ChatG or Perplexity or any AI tool, they take that one query and they fan it out. They spread it out into multiple other queries. So, you might look for the best running shoes, but then chat GPT might search for best running shoes 2026 in the background. So, what's happened is a lot of SEOs um they're saying we need to create content that matches the fan out. So they want to create content for all of these different variations of keywords. But then you get some um GEO companies or AEO companies and whatever you want to call them. All they do is help you scale content. So um they will help you rank for top ofunnel keywords. They will say you can automate these processes. You need to create a blog post on this and this. And what's happened is multiple websites are using those tools and they've just scaled their content. they've gone from having a hundred pages in their blog to having a thousand pages in their blog within weeks and that's not sustainable initially. They all see an increase in traffic or most of them see a big increase in traffic. Um and then the companies take that increase in traffic and say that oh we've increased AI visibility for this brand by 300%. But then comes along the crash where the keywords that you know they started ranking um they start to decline and we've named that in SEO that's been named as um Mount AI um rank and tank. There's many of different terms. So yeah, I'd say it's dangerous because the if your website gets hit by a Google algorithm update, it can take many years to recover. And that's not an understatement. There's so many case studies out there where you know some websites do take 2 3 years to recover. Why take that risk in the first place for traffic that doesn't mean anything? A lot of these tools, they're just making keywords like how to do something or like um or what is or you know explain this this topic explained that content is not generating revenue. It's not generating sales. I believe you have a course um compact keywords. The whole premise of that course is you want to rank for stuff that makes you money. This method of marketing is so effective, I had to make sure it wasn't against Google's rules before I kept doing it. It's a form of SEO I call compact keywords. Whereas most SEO focuses on putting up articles to answer questions, how, what, when, compact keywords focuses on putting up dozens of pages that sell to searchers who are actually looking to buy. These pages rank on Google and convert so much better than normal that when I discovered this years ago, I couldn't believe this was allowed. It's less work, too. The average Compact Keywords page is only 415 words. Compact Keywords is a 13-hour deep course on getting sales with SEO. A customer recently said, "Each lesson is dense with information. You're giving years worth of experience boiled down into 15 to 30 minute lessons with no filler or fluff. I feel like I'm gaining a new superpower. Compact Keywords is about setting up an SEO funnel that brings you sales for years and years and years. It works with AI. It's less work than traditional SEO and it makes way more money. You can get it now at compact keywords.com. Back to the podcast. Some of these GEO tactics, it deviates from that. You're just getting traffic for the sake of traffic. And a lot of the citations are fake. So, it sounds like I'm going on a rant here, but you can rank or show up in AI for an infinite number of terms, and one page can be cited for an infinite number of terms. So, let's just take a keyword how to get rid of mold. You can easily make that page with um with with AI, but how to when you take the how to get rid of mold within AI citations, there's yeah, there's so many ways that that URL can show up. So if it's coming from a brand, you can say how to get how to get rid of mold brand name. That's going to show up in AI citations and you'll be able to say that oh we've increased AI citations for this topic cluster, but that doesn't mean that you're more visible in AI. So I think the whole system of like measuring measuring citations, measuring the way brands show up in AI tools, I think it's dangerous and they're obviously just trying to sell their tools and sell their methods. But yeah, I personally wouldn't advise it. I don't think it's safe if there's multiple case studies out there where it's not um where it's not where um you know, yeah, companies have ranked and then and then tanked. >> So, you're saying that you're going to use these tactics, you're going to scale content for from 100 pages, 100 blog posts to the 1,000 plus blog posts. And this is going to get you a lot of organic traffic. And then it's going to get and you're going to get cited in AI. it's going to get you a lot of traffic from Google and you're going to get cited in AI. But and then you're saying but then you know Google is going to catch on to the patterns. You're going to get deranked. Your site is going to basically get hit by like a penalty. And uh that's going to be really bad for your organic traffic. But if I'm uh if I just care about generative engine optimization, if I just want to show up in AI, why is that even a problem? It's a problem because AI systems use search APIs to um get in to um to rank pages or to show pages. Um so it's it's quite common. I think it's it's common knowledge now within the AI industry that um yeah chatbt claude when they go and search the web they use an API that links to a search engine database. Whether that's Google, whether that's Bing, there's lots of different debates out there. um they use a search engine database to retrieve URLs. There's also many studies that show correlations between the better you rank in traditional search engines on Google and Bing, the better your chances your pages being retrieved when AI goes and searches searches the web. >> Is that often or or can like a company try to get into the to LLM's training data? >> You can. So that's the whole So the GEO tactics being and it's good you actually brought that up. So the tactics being promoted by these companies about create more content that is not going to get you into the LM training data. Getting into L&M training data, I personally don't think there's any true case study of any company doing it. Um because you have to compare output between models. So, if we want to get into the LLM training data, you have to ask AI to give you answers without searching the web because that's the only way you're going to know if the model has learned about you. Now, I've tried this. I'm not going to name drop the company, but um 2 years ago, around 2 years ago, um this company had a lot of negativity around how long their solution takes to implement for for enterprise companies. um they were pulling from G2, they were pulling from Reddit, they were pulling from other places around the internet where the LLM didn't even have to go make a search. It said, "Oh, for an enterprise, this solution can take 9 plus months to implement."
